Figure 2:  Illustration of the matching process of a static priority policy. The blue dots indicate the number of agents of each type that are available to match when a new agent of type  j j  arrives. Since the highest-priority types ( 5 5  and  4 4 ) are not available, the arriving agent matches to an agent of type  3 3 . If no acceptable agents were available, the arriving agent would wait.

Figure 3:  An example with three types and five arriving agents. Given the history shown on the left, the corresponding graph  G ⁡ ( t ) G(t)  is shown in the middle, with edge weights determined by the match rewards. There are two maximum-weight matchings:  { ( A , B ) , ( C , D ) } \{(A,B),(C,D)\}  and  { ( B , C ) , ( D , E ) } \{(B,C),(D,E)\} , both with weight  15 15 ;  OMN ​ ( t ) \textup{OMN}(t)  is the expected weight of a maximum-weight matching of  G ⁡ ( t ) G(t) , divided by  t t .

Figure 4:  Illustration of a static priority policy on the same example from  Figure   3 , with five agents belonging to three types. The policy is given in the box on the right. The middle panel explains how the policy operates on this example; the policy’s only match, between  B B  and  C C , is highlighted in red in the graph on the left. The policy earns a total reward of 10, whereas the maximum possible reward is 15. The best choice of policy depends on the arrival rates, departure rates, and rewards. We show how to identify a policy that earns at least half of the omniscient benchmark.
